lead.headline: Washington Unveils Tariffs on 14 Economies and Hot US Inflation Locks In a Fed Hike, Yet Wall Street Claws Back a Deep Drop and Asia Rebounds
lead.dek: Core PCE ran at 3.3% and Q3 growth was revised to 4.3%, leaving a 9 December Fed hike about 98% priced; USTR proposed Section 301 duties from 15% for the EU to as much as 35% for Vietnam; the Dow erased an 1,100-point slide to close above 50,000, and Brent jumped 3.5% to $94.61.
body: Wednesday packed three shocks into one session before Thanksgiving. The Commerce Department reported October core PCE inflation at 3.3%, a tenth above forecasts and the highest since 2023, with headline PCE at 3.8% and third-quarter GDP revised up to a 4.3% annual pace from 3.4% (25 Nov). CME FedWatch put the odds of a quarter-point hike at the 8-9 December meeting at 97.8%. Yet Treasuries rallied, with the 10-year yield down about 6bp to 4.85% and the 2-year at 4.61% (25 Nov close).

At the same time the US Trade Representative closed its excess-capacity probes into 16 economies and proposed new Section 301 tariffs on 14 of them: 15% for the EU, up to 15% for Japan, Korea, Switzerland and Taiwan, up to 20% for China and Singapore, up to 25% for India and up to 35% for Vietnam, with lower rates on offer for India (17%), Singapore (10%) and Vietnam (20%) under trade deals. Nothing takes effect yet: comments are due 5 January 2027 and hearings start 25 January. Brussels, Beijing, New Delhi, Taipei and Singapore all pushed back on Thursday.

Equities swung hard. The Nasdaq was down about 3.2% and the Dow more than 1,100 points early as chip stocks slid again, before dip-buyers lifted all three gauges off their lows: the Dow closed up 0.33% at 50,182.95, the S&P 500 down 0.25% at 7,182.78 and the Nasdaq down 0.62% at 23,585.80, with the VIX up 7.3% to 28.29 (25 Nov close). Nvidia still lost 3.9%. Europe fared worse, closing before the rebound: the STOXX 600 fell about 1% to 626.03 and banks about 3%, as markets priced an 87% chance of an ECB hike in December.

Oil added a fourth front. Brent swung from about $89.82 in the European morning to a $94.61 settle, up 3.5%, after Yemen's Houthis said they targeted Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery (Saudi forces said they downed four drones) while Iran reported more tankers hitting mines near Hormuz. On Thursday Asia took its cue from Wall Street's recovery: the Hang Seng rose about 2.5%, the Taiex 2% and the Nikkei 1.5% in early trade (about 03:45 CET), and the Bank of Korea raised its rate to 3.25%. US markets are closed today and trade a half-day on Friday.

impact.title: What it means for markets
points: A December Fed hike is effectively priced, so the next repricing is about January and March: hot core inflation alongside 4.3% growth keeps the higher-for-longer path in play for long-duration growth stocks, even though Treasuries rallied on the day.

The tariff proposals are a 2027 risk, not an immediate cost: rates for the EU, Japan, Korea and Taiwan sit near their existing 15% deal caps, while Vietnam, India and other ASEAN exporters carry the steepest proposed rates and the most negotiating risk for their currencies and export sectors.
Oil's war premium is back after Brent's lowest close since August on 23 Nov; Gulf shipping, war-risk insurance and refiners are the most sensitive channels, with OPEC+ meeting on 29 Nov.

Global tightening is broadening: the Bank of Korea hiked today, markets price ECB and BoJ moves in December, and India's RBI decides on 4 December, which weighs on rate-sensitive bank stocks, as Europe's 3% bank sell-off showed.

read.title: The Ledger's Read
paragraphs: Wednesday's session showed how much bad news is already in prices. A hotter-than-expected core PCE print and a big upward revision to growth should have been poison for a market that had just lost faith in the AI trade, and for an hour it was: the Nasdaq was down more than 3%. But the December Fed hike was already almost fully priced, Treasuries rallied rather than sold off, and buyers stepped in before the holiday. The Dow's close above 50,000 again says the money is rotating toward cyclicals and value, while chipmakers, from Nvidia to Micron and Lam Research, still carry the selling.

The tariff notices are the story with the longest tail. By keeping the EU, Japan, Korea and Taiwan near their existing 15% caps, Washington signalled continuity for its deal partners and pressure on those without deals: Vietnam, India and Singapore get a higher headline rate and an explicit discount for signing. That makes the comment period to 5 January a negotiating window, and exporters' currencies and export-heavy indices in those economies the most exposed. Europe's 3% bank sell-off was about rates more than tariffs, as ECB hike odds near 87%, but it shows how quickly the global tightening theme, now joined by Korea's hike and hawkish BoJ talk, reaches equities.

Oil is the wild card for inflation. Brent's $5 intraday swing came from the Red Sea, not Hormuz, as the Houthis aimed at Saudi energy assets, while Iran's blockade stand-off shows no sign of resolution. A sustained move above the mid-$90s would feed the very inflation that is pushing central banks to hike. Watch Friday's thin US half-day, Tokyo CPI, OPEC+ on 29 November, India's GDP on 30 November and the Huang hearings from 1 December.

stories.summary: The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed up 164.25 points, or 0.33%, at 50,182.95 on Wednesday (25 Nov close) after having been down more than 1,100 points during the session. The S&P 500 slipped 0.25% to 7,182.78 and the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.62% to 23,585.80, a fraction of the losses seen at the open, when the Nasdaq was down about 3.2% and the S&P 500 about 2.1%. The early slide came as hotter-than-expected core inflation and a fresh AI-chip sell-off hit at the same time; late dip-buying then lifted all three gauges off their lows. The Russell 2000 gained 0.71% to 2,704.06, while the VIX rose 7.3% to 28.29 (25 Nov close). US markets are shut on Thursday for Thanksgiving and trade a half-day to 1 p.m. ET on Friday.
stories.market: Energy led sector gains and defensives such as Charter (+8.4%) outperformed, while chipmakers and consumer discretionary lagged; HP rose 11.5% on results (25 Nov close). A VIX near 28 signals that options traders still price large swings into thin holiday trading.

body: Wednesday's session was a study in reversals. Stocks opened sharply lower: according to Yahoo Finance's live coverage, the Nasdaq Composite was down about 3.2% and the S&P 500 about 2.1% at the open, and the Dow had dropped more than 1,100 points at its worst. By the close the Dow was up 0.33% at 50,182.95, holding above the 50,000 mark it first cleared earlier in the week, while the S&P 500 ended 0.25% lower at 7,182.78 and the Nasdaq 0.62% lower at 23,585.80 (25 Nov close).

Two forces drove the early sell-off. October's core PCE price index rose 3.3% from a year earlier, slightly above the 3.2% consensus, while third-quarter GDP growth was revised up to a 4.3% annual rate from 3.4%. Together they cemented expectations of a Federal Reserve rate increase on 9 December. At the same time, renewed doubts about returns on AI spending sent the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index down more than 6% in the afternoon at one point, and Yahoo Finance noted that the Nasdaq-100 was briefly on course for a close in bear-market territory.

The recovery came late and was broad among defensive and cyclical names. Energy was the best-performing sector; HP Inc. rose 11.49% after its results and outlook, Charter Communications 8.39% and Deere about 4.4% after an early drop on its forecast. On the downside, Ambarella fell 19.77% and Nutanix about 15.2% on guidance, Urban Outfitters 10.3% and Nvidia 3.91% to $149.30 (25 Nov close).

Small caps outperformed, with the Russell 2000 up 0.71%, and Treasury yields fell, with the 10-year down about 6 basis points to 4.85%. Volatility stayed high: the VIX rose 7.32% to 28.29. Strategists also had new US tariff proposals to digest, as Washington outlined Section 301 duties of up to 20% on China, the EU and a dozen other partners, subject to comments and hearings into January.
US exchanges are closed on Thursday 26 November for Thanksgiving; Friday is a shortened session ending at 1 p.m. ET, and normal hours resume on Monday 30 November.

body: Wednesday's data dump left little doubt about the Fed's next step. Headline PCE inflation rose to 3.8% year on year in October, in line with forecasts, and core PCE to 3.3%, a tenth above expectations. On the month both rose 0.3%. Personal income rose 0.7% against a 0.4% forecast, spending rose 0.3% and the saving rate was 4.1%, according to Coin Alert News. Q3 GDP was revised up to 4.3% annualised, well above the 3.5% expected.

CME FedWatch put the probability of a 25bp hike on 9 December at 97.8% at the close, up from about 91% on 23 November, per Admiral Markets. Polymarket showed 94% and Kalshi 92-93%. For the 28 January 2027 meeting, prediction markets were roughly evenly split to modestly in favour of another increase.

Bond markets took the data in stride. The 10-year Treasury yield fell about 6 basis points to 4.85% and the 2-year 2bp to 4.61% (25 Nov close), helped by the late equity rebound and holiday positioning. The 30-year was about 5.24%.

Fed officials have been split on the size of the move. Governor Christopher Waller has argued that 50bp should be considered if core inflation runs near 0.3% a month again, while New York Fed President John Williams has said the situation does not call for dramatic action, according to Admiral Markets' summary. RSM's Joseph Brusuelas said the Fed is locked in for December and the question is whether it continues in January and March.

stories.headline: Bank of Korea Raises Rates to 3.25% in a 5-2 Vote and Lifts Its 2027 Growth Forecast to 4.1%
stories.summary: The Bank of Korea raised its base rate by 25bp to 3.25% on Thursday (26 Nov), its third hike of 2026 and the highest level since late 2024, as 32 of 34 economists polled by Reuters had expected. Two board members, Hwang Kun-il and Lee Soo-hyung, voted to hold at 3%. The bank raised its 2026 growth forecast to 3.9% from 3.3% and its 2027 forecast to 4.1% from 2.9%, citing strong semiconductor exports, and lifted its 2027 inflation forecast to 2.4%. Governor Shin Hyun Song said inflation is not expected to return to 2% until the year after next.
stories.market: The statement dropped the word 'pace' from its guidance on further increases, read by some as a mildly dovish signal; three-year government bond futures fell 0.18 points to 103.83 (03:35 GMT, 26 Nov) while the Kospi traded about 1.2% higher.

body: The Bank of Korea resumed tightening on Thursday after pausing in October, raising its seven-day repo rate by a quarter point to 3.25%. That brings cumulative tightening this year to 75bp, after hikes in July and August. The decision, at the last meeting of 2026, was widely expected.

The vote was 5-2, with board members Hwang Kun-il and Lee Soo-hyung preferring to hold at 3%. The bank sharply upgraded its outlook: growth is now forecast at 3.9% for 2026 (from 3.3%) and 4.1% for 2027 (from 2.9%), the fastest since 2021, on the back of booming chip exports. It sees inflation averaging 2.7% this year and 2.4% next.

Governor Shin Hyun Song said sticky inflation reflects upstream cost pressure as well as robust domestic demand, and argued that acting early could limit the total tightening needed. Board members were split almost evenly on whether rates will be 3.25%, 3.50% or 3.75% in six months.

The statement now says the board will decide on the timing of further increases, having previously referred to both timing and pace. Kyobo Securities' Paik Yoon-min read that as a sign the cycle may end after one or two more moves, and most analysts expect a final hike in the first quarter of 2027 to a 3.50% peak.

analysts.view: Wording change suggests the cycle ends after one or two more moves; still expects a Q1 2027 hike

detail.consensus: Analysts broadly expect one final quarter-point hike in Q1 2027 to 3.50%, then a hold.

stories.headline: Brent Swings Almost $5 in a Day, From Below $90 to a $94.61 Settle, as Houthis Target Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura
stories.summary: Brent crude settled up $3.21, or 3.5%, at $94.61 a barrel on Wednesday and WTI rose 2% to $83.68 (25 Nov settle), after Brent had traded as low as about $89.82 in European morning trade. The turn came as Yemen's Houthis said they targeted Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery and Riyadh's financial district; Saudi forces said they intercepted four drones aimed at Ras Tanura. Brent held near $94.60 in early Asian trade on Thursday (02:29 GMT). US crude stocks rose 1.1 million barrels to 418.9 million, a smaller build than the 1.5 million expected.
stories.market: Energy was the best-performing S&P 500 sector on Wednesday; higher oil also feeds the inflation debate that is driving Fed hike bets. OPEC+ meets on Sunday 29 Nov to set 2027 output policy.

body: Oil had a volatile session on Wednesday. In the European morning Brent was down 1.73% at $89.82, Anadolu Agency reported, as recovering Gulf exports and forecasts of a fourth-quarter surplus weighed. By the settlement it was up 3.5% at $94.61, the highest in more than a week, and WTI was up 2% at $83.68 (25 Nov settle).

The trigger was a fresh round of attacks. Yemen's Houthis said they targeted Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery and export complex and Riyadh's financial district; a person familiar with the matter confirmed the refinery attack to Reuters, and Saudi forces said four drones were intercepted. Iran also claimed more mine strikes on tankers near the Strait of Hormuz, which could not be independently verified. Short-covering before the Thanksgiving holiday amplified the move.

US data were mildly supportive: the EIA reported a 1.1 million-barrel rise in commercial crude stocks to 418.9 million for the week to 20 November, less than the 1.5 million expected, while crude exports fell about 1.2 million barrels a day to 3.3 million.

Early on Thursday, Brent was unchanged at $94.60 and WTI up 0.3% at $83.90 (02:29 GMT), after a near-6% gain over two sessions. ANZ estimates Hormuz throughput at only about 49% of normal, with low inventories and almost no spare capacity, while Standard Chartered's Emily Ashford said much of the expected normalisation appears priced in.

body: Gold's reaction to Wednesday's US data was a round trip. Spot prices initially fell 1-2% after the upward GDP revision and hotter core PCE reinforced bets on a December Fed hike, which raises the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding bullion.

Spot gold ended late US trading up 0.6% at $3,576.30 and was near $3,571 on Thursday morning, according to Mitrade. Gold futures were up 0.29% at $3,572.40, the Motley Fool reported (25 Nov).

stories.headline: Rupee Rises 69 Paise to 92.23 per Dollar, Its Strongest in Eight Months, on Foreign Equity Inflows
stories.summary: The Indian rupee strengthened 69 paise to close at 92.23 per dollar on Wednesday (25 Nov close), an eight-month high, after touching 92.18 intraday. Ten straight sessions of foreign buying of Indian equities, including Rs 5,672.99 crore on 23 Nov, and lower crude during India's trading day supported the currency. stories.market: A firmer rupee eases imported-inflation pressure from oil and supports foreign returns on Indian assets; the risk is crude's late rebound to $94.61 after India's close.

body: The rupee had its best day in weeks on Wednesday, gaining 69 paise to close at 92.23 per dollar, its strongest in about eight months, according to HDFC Sky. It touched 92.18 intraday.

Foreign portfolio inflows were the main driver: foreign institutional investors bought a net Rs 5,672.99 crore of Indian shares on 23 November, extending their buying to ten sessions. Brent's dip below $90 during the Indian session also helped, as oil is India's largest import.

The Reserve Bank of India ran a second Rs 500 billion overnight repo auction, Wellstrack reported, adding liquidity at a time when the Fed is expected to tighten. In the US, the dollar index slipped 0.1% to 103.71 (25 Nov close).

stories.headline: Washington Proposes Section 301 Tariffs on 14 Economies, From 15% for the EU and Japan to as Much as 35% for Vietnam; Mexico and Norway Spared for Now
stories.summary: The US Trade Representative on 25 Nov published determinations in its structural-excess-capacity probes and proposed new tariffs on 14 of the 16 economies it began investigating on 11 March. Proposed rates (net of existing Section 301 duties) are 15% for the EU, up to 15% for Japan, South Korea, Switzerland and Taiwan, up to 18% for Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand, up to 20% for China and Singapore, up to 25% for India and up to 35% for Vietnam. Mexico and Norway received no determination for now. Lower rates are on offer for India (17%), Singapore (10%) and Vietnam (20%) if they reach reciprocal trade agreements, while partners with existing deals face higher fallback rates if their commitments disappoint. Nothing takes effect yet: written comments are due 5 Jan 2027 and hearings start 25 Jan 2027.
stories.market: The proposals land with US markets shut for Thanksgiving; exporters in Vietnam, India and other ASEAN economies carry the steepest proposed rates, while the EU, Japan, Korea and Taiwan see rates consistent with their 15% deal caps. The STOXX 600 was up 0.5% at 636.01 (0819 GMT, 25 Nov) as investors awaited the findings.

sources.name: Curtis, Mallet-Prevost trade law blog, 25 Nov

body: The USTR's notices close out the excess-capacity investigations opened in March, after the Supreme Court struck down the earlier emergency-powers (IEEPA) tariffs in February and a temporary 10% Section 122 tariff ran its 150-day course to late July. The new duties would come on top of the forced-labour Section 301 tariffs that have applied since 24 July.

For economies that already have trade arrangements with Washington, the lower number is the proposal and a higher fallback applies if USTR judges their commitments unsatisfactory: up to 40% for China, up to 25% for Korea, Taiwan, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand, and up to 20% for the EU, Japan, Switzerland and Bangladesh. For India, Singapore and Vietnam, which have not concluded such agreements, the higher number is the proposal and USTR says it would consider 17%, 10% and 20% respectively under a deal.

China's proposal is split: up to 20% on goods outside the annexes, up to 10% on goods in Annex A, and no new tariff on Annex B goods, with USTR tying the structure to the October 2025 Kuala Lumpur arrangement. Each economy also has product exemptions listed in annexes to the Federal Register notices.

A senior US official said the rates are meant to stay consistent with signed deals, including the 15% cap agreed by the EU, Japan, Korea and Taiwan (Taipei Times, 26 Nov). None of the notices sets an effective date; USTR says it would 'consider applying' the duties after the comment process.
Separately, a Court of International Trade panel heard argument on 30 Sept in a challenge to the July forced-labour Section 301 tariffs and has not yet ruled (as of 25 Nov).

stories.headline: Brussels Rejects the Overcapacity Charge, Taipei Says the Rates Are Not Final, and Seoul's Bill Would Rise to 15%
stories.summary: European Commission spokesman Olof Gill on 26 Nov rejected the US finding that Europe is a source of excess capacity, arguing the EU is itself among the economies most exposed to it and criticising the lack of joint action. In Taipei, Executive Yuan spokeswoman Michelle Lee said the US still has to hold hearings before setting final rates and that Taiwan expects the outcome to reflect its earlier bilateral deal, with officials looking for a 15% non-stacked total. For South Korea, USTR proposed a 2.5% overcapacity tariff on top of the 12.5% forced-labour duty in place since 24 July, taking the total to 15%, but warned it could return to 25% if Seoul's $350 billion investment pledge falls short. China's foreign ministry urged that disputes be settled through equal consultation.
stories.market: Partners with 15% caps look broadly protected for now, which limits the hit to European, Korean and Taiwanese exporters; USTR's report singles out Korean autos, semiconductors and petrochemicals, keeping the 25% fallback risk on Samsung Electronics and SK hynix in view.

body: The EU's proposed rate is 15%, inclusive of ordinary customs duties and existing Section 301 tariffs, with product exemptions; the fallback if commitments disappoint is up to 20%. Gill said Washington and Brussels share concerns about overcapacity elsewhere and should act together rather than target each other (26 Nov).

Taiwan has signed an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade and an investment memorandum with the US. A Taiwan Institute of Economic Research official estimated the US could add about 5% for overcapacity on top of Taiwan's 10% forced-labour rate, which would still leave the total at 15% (Taipei Times, 26 Nov).

USTR's Korea findings cite industrial plans, policy-finance loans and tax support, pointing to the semiconductor cluster in the Gwangju-Jeolla region and to Samsung and SK hynix's memory market shares. The report says Korea's rate could go back to 25% if fulfilment of its $350 billion investment pledge and other commitments is judged unsatisfactory (Seoul Economic Daily, 26 Nov).
The Seoul Economic Daily also reported that USTR is weighing separate Section 301 probes into digital policies in Korea, the EU and Australia, which could push totals above 15%.

stories.headline: US Proposes Ending Brazil's Aircraft Exemption With a 10% Duty and Tightens Sugar Access; Brasília Expresses 'Outrage'
stories.summary: USTR on 25 Nov proposed a 10% tariff on finished Brazilian aircraft, which have been exempt, and a new rate on out-of-quota raw and refined sugar aimed at stopping Brazilian sugar arriving via third countries. Aircraft are Brazil's fourth-largest export to the US. The US also plans to cut Brazil's tariff-free raw-sugar quota for 2027 by about a third to 100,000 tonnes. Brazil's government called the move unacceptable and said it was meant to pressure it over the Pix payments system and digital trade; a USTR hearing is set for 14 Jan 2027.
stories.market: Embraer shares fell more than 3% on Wednesday afternoon (25 Nov); US regional airlines that rely on Embraer jets would face higher costs if the duty is imposed.

body: USTR Jamieson Greer said the office was revising tariffs imposed on Brazil in July because Brasília had made no meaningful progress, while saying Washington remains open to talks. The July package kept and widened exemptions for Brazilian beef, coffee and aircraft.
Brazil also faces a separate 12.5% forced-labour Section 301 tariff. The Supreme Court in February struck down the earlier emergency tariffs, which had reached 50% on some Brazilian goods.

On Tuesday 24 Nov Brazil asked the WTO to set up a dispute panel on the July tariffs; the US blocked the request the same day. Embraer said it is reviewing the proposal and backs the zero-tariff regime that has governed civil aerospace since the 1980s.
Brazilian sugar exports to the US fell to just over 146,000 tonnes in 2026 through October, from more than 1 million tonnes in 2024, according to industry group UNICA.

stories.summary: Yair Golan's Democrats on 25 Nov suspended coalition talks with Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar, saying there was no point while Yashar keeps negotiating with Netanyahu's Likud, and demanded the unity option be taken off the table. His bloc won 67 seats in the 27 Oct election, including 19 held by Arab parties, versus 53 for Netanyahu's bloc.

stories.headline: Iran War, Day 272: Tehran Says Two More Tankers Hit Mines and Ties Hormuz's Reopening to the US Blockade, as Brent Jumps 3.5%
stories.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards navy said on 25 Nov that two oil tankers using an unauthorised route struck mines off the strait's southern and eastern coasts and caught fire, and Iran's army said a tanker that had switched off its tracking systems was hit in a restricted zone; Reuters could not verify the accounts. Tehran says normal shipping will not resume until the US naval blockade of its ports is lifted and the war ends, and has offered via Qatar to reopen the waterway within 48 hours of those conditions being met. IMF PortWatch logged just one transit on 22 Nov against a pre-crisis norm of about 85 a day. Trump said on 25 Nov that US military funding for the war runs to about the end of January. Brent settled 3.5% higher at $94.61 on 25 Nov and held near that level in early Asian trade on 26 Nov.
stories.market: Mine claims plus Houthi strikes on Saudi ports and the Ras Tanura area gave Brent a third straight gain, pulling it back from its lowest close since August; war-risk insurance, tanker rates and Gulf equities remain the most exposed channels, while a forecast fourth-quarter surplus and OPEC+'s 29 Nov meeting cap the rally.

body: Iran reported a fresh run of mine incidents on 25 Nov. The IRGC navy said two tankers that ignored its traffic-control instructions exploded and caught fire in their engine rooms off the southern and eastern coasts of the strait, following three similar claims earlier in the week. Separately, Iran's army, via Fars, said a tanker hit a mine in a 'restricted zone'; Iran's navy later said a vessel that had turned off its identification and navigation systems caught fire and stopped east of the strait. Reuters could not independently verify the claims, and no vessel names were given.

Army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said new surveillance and control systems have been deployed and that ships not coordinating with Iranian forces face greater risk. Tehran repeats that normal traffic depends on Washington lifting its naval blockade of Iranian ports and the war ending on all fronts, and it has told Qatari mediators it could reopen the waterway within 48 hours of those conditions being met.

Traffic remains a fraction of normal: IMF PortWatch recorded one transit on 22 Nov against a pre-crisis baseline of 85 a day, and Bloomberg data cited by PiQ show tanker attacks running at a near-daily pace in November after an October peak.

In Washington, Trump said on 25 Nov that funding for the military campaign lasts until roughly the end of January and warned that the incoming Democratic Congress could push to end it early. Iran's foreign minister accused Israel of trying to drag the US into a new round of war over a chemical-weapons claim, and the US mission to the UAE issued a security alert after reported Iranian attacks on US assets in Bahrain and Kuwait.

Oil reacted: Brent rose about 3% on 25 Nov and was quoted near $94-95 late in the day (Straits, Trading Economics), its third straight gain, after the mine reports and Houthi claims against Saudi targets. Trading Economics showed it about 0.7% higher near $95.2 early on 26 Nov. Offsetting forces include recovering Gulf crude shipments, an IEA-projected fourth-quarter surplus and OPEC+'s 29 Nov meeting on 2027 output; Brent is still down nearly 20% in November.

stories.headline: Houthis Hit Saudi Arabia's Jazan Port and Send a Drone at Jeddah After Saudi Raids on Hodeidah, and Claim a Strike on Ras Tanura
stories.summary: The Houthis carried out their threat against Saudi Red Sea ports on 25 Nov: a projectile hit Jazan port, causing minor damage and no injuries, and a drone was shot down over Jeddah Islamic Port, the Saudi-led coalition said. The attacks followed coalition strikes on Hodeidah port that hit storage tanks and cranes, after the coalition told civilians to evacuate. Saudi air defences destroyed four drones over Ras Tanura, home to the kingdom's largest refinery and a key export terminal; the Houthis claimed fires there, which Riyadh has not confirmed. The coalition also intercepted ballistic missiles aimed at Riyadh, and India said two of its nationals were among 11 hurt at the PIF Tower on 24 Nov.
stories.market: Attacks on Jazan and Jeddah and the Ras Tanura claim helped lift Brent about 3% on 25 Nov; with Hormuz shut, Saudi Arabia leans on Red Sea ports such as Jeddah and Yanbu, so war-risk costs for those routes and Saudi equities are the main channels.

body: The Saudi-led coalition struck Hodeidah port on 25 Nov after warning civilians to leave, saying it hit operational capabilities there and targets in Saada and Amran. Al Jazeera reported damage to storage tanks and cargo cranes at a port that handles about 90% of Yemen's imported goods, raising humanitarian concerns.

The Houthis, who had warned that Jeddah and all Saudi Red Sea ports would be targeted if Hodeidah was hit and told shipping firms to withdraw vessels, then said they attacked Jazan and Jeddah. The coalition said a projectile caused minor damage at Jazan and a drone was destroyed near Jeddah Islamic Port, with no civilian injuries reported.

Earlier on 25 Nov, Saudi air defences destroyed four drones over Ras Tanura with fragments falling but no casualties initially reported; the Houthis claimed their strikes on the refinery and on Riyadh's financial district caused fires. The coalition also said it intercepted ballistic missiles aimed at the capital.

The Houthis banned shipping to and from Saudi ports in July, and clashes intensified after their September advance toward Bab el-Mandeb. On the ground, Yemen's government said its forces conducted 654 strikes on Houthi positions on 25 Nov, with the heaviest fighting on the western Taiz front, while the Houthis said the coalition launched 105 air and missile strikes on Sanaa and 10 governorates the same day.

stories.headline: Israel Kills a Second Hamas Security Chief in Two Days as the UN Rights Chief Warns of Atrocity Risk
stories.summary: Israeli strikes killed Hamas's northern Gaza security chief on 25 Nov, a day after killing the group's internal security head, and a separate strike killed a Hamas deputy education minister and his wife, the Times of Israel reported on 26 Nov. UN human rights chief Volker Türk warned on 25 Nov of a growing risk of atrocity crimes against Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank. US envoy Kushner said Israel must leave its wartime mindset as the Board of Peace accuses Netanyahu of blocking its plan to disarm Hamas. In Lebanon, a judge issued arrest warrants for five detained Hezbollah members.
stories.market: Direct market impact is low, but the strains feed into Israel's coalition politics and defence spending, and Lebanon's distressed bonds; Kushner floated Sinai data-centre and energy projects if Gaza is resolved.

body: Israel's campaign against Hamas commanders continued under the October 2025 truce. After killing internal security chief Naeem Abu Nahel on 24 Nov, Israeli forces killed the group's security chief for northern Gaza on 25 Nov, and a strike that the military said targeted a senior militant killed a Hamas deputy education minister and his wife.

Diplomatic pressure is building. UN rights chief Volker Türk warned of a rising risk of atrocity crimes in Gaza and the West Bank. Netanyahu and Kushner spoke by phone about Gaza's humanitarian situation, a day after Kushner warned Israel risks becoming a pariah; the Board of Peace, which Kushner designed, says Netanyahu is blocking its Hamas disarmament plan. Kushner also said a new Palestinian technocratic administration has been set up to replace Hamas temporarily.

In Israel, lawmakers gave preliminary approval, 65-50, to a bill for a state inquiry into the 7 October attack. In Lebanon, a judge issued arrest warrants for five detained Hezbollah members and summoned three others for questioning, as Beirut presses for an Israeli withdrawal and Hezbollah's disarmament.

stories.headline: Ukraine Sets Two Samara Refineries Ablaze and Hits Five Jets, as Russian Shelling Cuts the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Plant's Outside Power
stories.summary: Ukraine's General Staff said on 25 Nov it struck two Rosneft refineries in Samara region, with monitoring channels naming the Kuibyshev and Syzran plants, while Samara's governor said more than 145 drones were downed; it also said five aircraft, reportedly three MiG-31s and two Su-34s, were hit at Savasleyka air base. Russian shelling cut the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant's external power, leaving it on diesel generators, and attacks killed 9 and injured 59 across Ukraine in a day, halting a thermal power plant. Poland said it will set up a no-fly zone on its Ukraine border. Kyiv Independent reported the US rules out troops or bases in Ukraine under post-war guarantees, while Peskov said no date is set for new talks.
stories.market: Each strike adds to the 45% cut in Russian refinery runs reported since late October, tightening diesel and gasoline exports more than crude; attacks on Ukraine's gas production and grid, and the 1 Jan EU ban on Russian seaborne LNG, keep TTF gas sensitive.

body: Ukraine widened its long-range campaign a day after Putin vowed 'inevitable' retaliation. The General Staff said it hit two oil refineries in Samara region together with a resistance group; Ukrainian monitors said Rosneft's Kuibyshev and Syzran plants were on fire, and the regional governor reported one death and more than 145 drones shot down. Kyiv also said it struck Savasleyka air base in Nizhny Novgorod region, hitting five jets, and Zelensky confirmed a drone strike on a Russian cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland.

Russia's strikes on Ukraine continued: the air force counted 112 drones overnight, attacks killed nine people and injured 59 over a day, a Naftogaz gas-production site in Poltava region was set ablaze and a thermal power plant stopped generating. Energoatom said shelling cut the Ferrosplavna-1 line, leaving the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant on backup diesel power, and large parts of Zaporizhzhia, Mykolaiv and Odesa regions lost electricity.

Poland said it will create a no-fly zone along its border with Ukraine after Russian missiles and drones entered its airspace on 23-24 Nov, and asked NATO to intercept missiles over Ukraine; NATO is opposed. Finland and Norway pledged nearly $60 million for energy repairs, and a study put the cost of a year-long Black Sea port blockade at $9.8 billion in 2027, or 4.1% of GDP.

On diplomacy, Zelensky said Washington is pressing for a deal by January, the Kyiv Independent reported that the US rules out troops and bases under post-war guarantees, and Peskov said no date is set for the next trilateral round. Budanov said a prisoner exchange of more than 1,000 people could come in late November or early December.

stories.headline: RSF Drone Swarm Kills at Least 17 in Damazin and Roseires, Targeting Power Facilities Near Sudan's Biggest Dam
stories.summary: More than 40 suicide drones struck Ed Damazin, the Blue Nile state capital, and nearby El Roseires late on 24 Nov, the Blue Nile Civil Society Initiative said, killing 17 and injuring 20 in its revised count; the Emergency Lawyers group put the toll at 19 and said electricity facilities in Damazin and the Roseires dam area were targeted. A military source blamed the RSF, and authorities imposed a 22:00-05:00 curfew. The RSF and allied SPLM-N forces now hold small towns 65-70 km from Damazin, while the army pushes the RSF back in West Kordofan, The National reported on 25 Nov.
stories.market: The Roseires hydroelectric dam is one of Sudan's main power sources, and Blue Nile borders Ethiopia and South Sudan; gold output and cross-border trade are the main economic channels, though gold prices are driven by global factors.

body: The overnight attack was one of the heaviest on Blue Nile's main towns. Drones hit residential districts of Ed Damazin, setting homes on fire and targeting the army's 4th Infantry Division headquarters; in El Saliha, west of the city, a strike killed members of three families. In El Roseires, a public viewing hall and nearby homes were hit. Casualty counts rose through the day, from an initial 15 to 17 dead and 20 injured per the civil-society group, with the state government citing 16 dead including seven women and two children.

Emergency Lawyers said drones also targeted electricity facilities in Damazin and the large dam at Roseires. Authorities imposed an overnight curfew and banned motorcycles other than security vehicles.

Analysts quoted by The National say the RSF is opening fronts far from the main western battles to stretch the army. RSF and SPLM-N forces have taken towns near the Ethiopian and South Sudanese borders, while the army still controls all of Blue Nile's main cities and is gradually pushing the RSF out of West Kordofan, possibly ahead of a campaign to retake Darfur. Army chief Burhan rejects any RSF role in Sudan's future, and foreign mediation is making little headway.
Drones are the war's main killer of civilians: about 80% of the 1,390 civilian deaths recorded in January-June 2026 were caused by drones, per figures cited by Al Jazeera.

stories.headline: German Q3 Growth Cut to 0.1% as Machinery Investment Drops 3.5% and Exports Fall
stories.summary: Germany's economy grew just 0.1% quarter on quarter in July-September, the statistics office said on 25 Nov, revising down its 30 Oct flash estimate of 0.2%; year-on-year growth was cut to 1.2% from 1.3%. Weaker September retail sales and exports drove the revision. Fixed investment fell 1.2%, with machinery and equipment down 3.5%, and exports dropped 1.0%, while household spending rose only 0.1% and government spending 0.3%. Employment fell by 222,000 (0.5%) from a year earlier to about 45.7 million.
stories.market: The soft detail contrasts with Monday's rise in Ifo business morale to 90.6 and keeps attention on whether Berlin's debt-financed 2027 budget lifts investment; German cyclicals and Bund yields are the most exposed assets.

body: Destatis said the downward revision came mainly from weaker retail trade and exports in September, data that were not available for the flash estimate published on 30 Oct.

Investment was the main drag on the quarter: gross fixed capital formation fell 1.2%, with machinery and equipment down 3.5% and construction down 0.3%. Exports of goods fell 0.8% and of services 1.7%, while imports dropped 1.4%, so net trade was not the main weight.
Consumption barely grew: household spending rose 0.1% and government spending 0.3% on the quarter. Year on year, total final consumption was up 0.9%, led by a 1.7% increase in government spending.
The labour market is softening: about 45.7 million people were in work, 222,000 fewer than a year earlier, and total hours worked fell 0.3%. Productivity per hour rose 1.5% year on year.

stories.headline: Merz Defends a Record €560 Billion 2027 Budget With €210 Billion of New Borrowing as the Audit Court Warns of a Debt Trap
stories.summary: The Bundestag began final deliberations on the 2027 federal budget on 24 Nov and held the general debate on 25 Nov over a record €560 billion spending plan financed with about €210 billion of new loans. The Federal Court of Audit has warned of a path into a debt trap, and critics note that nearly one in three euros of planned spending would be borrowed. CDU/CSU lawmaker Mathias Middelberg called for hard savings on state spending from 2028, starting with personnel costs, and defended roughly €11 billion of aid to Ukraine. The Left called the plan a debt binge and the Greens said it lacked foundations, while the AfD backed a planned 2027 electricity-tax cut but attacked its financing.
stories.market: Heavy federal borrowing adds to Bund supply and supports German infrastructure and defence names; a 2027 electricity-tax cut would ease costs for energy-intensive industry.

body: The general debate, traditionally the set-piece clash over the chancellor's budget, opened on Wednesday morning with the AfD, the largest opposition group. Chancellor Friedrich Merz was expected to address planning for 2028 and the case for continued Ukraine support.

The 2027 plan totals about €560 billion, the largest federal budget on record, with roughly €210 billion of new borrowing (ZDF, 25 Nov). The Federal Court of Audit has cautioned that the borrowing path risks a debt trap.

Middelberg (CDU/CSU) said the government must save sharply on state spending and wants tighter savings targets for 2028, beginning with personnel costs, alongside measures for growth. He described Ukraine aid of about €11 billion as the best investment Germany could make.

The AfD's Michael Espendiller said about €40 billion is spent from the Climate and Transformation Fund, much of it, in his view, without effect; he backed the electricity-tax cut but called its financing unserious.

stories.headline: EU Leaders Weigh €60 Billion a Year of New Bloc-Wide Taxes, From an E-Waste Levy to a Share of Carbon Revenue
stories.summary: As EU leaders negotiate the bloc's next seven-year budget, member states are discussing a package of new EU-wide revenue sources proposed by European Council President António Costa that would raise about €60 billion a year (Euronews, 26 Nov). The largest would be a levy of €2.25 per kg of uncollected electronic waste, expected to bring in more than €20 billion a year, alongside €1.25 per kg on non-recycled plastic packaging, a digital services tax, a tobacco excise share, 30% of Emissions Trading System revenue and carbon-border (CBAM) receipts. Commission projections for 2028-2034 show Germany paying the most at over €13 billion, ahead of Italy at €8 billion and France. No decision has been taken.
stories.market: A bloc-wide digital levy would affect large US tech platforms, while the e-waste and packaging levies touch electronics retailers and consumer-goods makers; France, Italy and Spain would give up their national digital-tax revenue to Brussels.

stories.headline: India Rejects the US Overcapacity Finding as Washington Proposes 25% Tariffs, or 17% With a Trade Deal
stories.summary: India's Commerce Ministry said on 26 Nov it is examining the USTR's Section 301 notice and rejected the claim of structural excess manufacturing capacity, saying it had already told Washington that India has none in any sector. USTR proposed tariffs of up to 25% on Indian goods but said it would consider 17% if India concludes a reciprocal trade agreement; the ministry said concerns should be settled in the bilateral talks and reaffirmed its aim of an early deal. At 17%, India would have a 1-point edge over Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand (18%) and 3 points over China and Vietnam's deal rate (20%). The Sensex opened 363 points higher at 84,301.40 on Thursday but slipped to 83,829.17 within the first half hour as the tariff risk weighed.
stories.market: Exporters in pharmaceuticals, steel and ICT goods, the sectors where USTR cited Indian surpluses, are most exposed; foreign investors have nonetheless poured a record $14.28 billion into Indian equities in November (as of 26 Nov report).

body: The ministry's statement stressed that India had engaged constructively in the investigation and that trade concerns should be resolved through the interim bilateral agreement now under negotiation. The framework for that deal was announced on 2 Feb and set out in a 7 Feb joint statement, then reopened after the Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs.
USTR's proposal for India is up to 25%, net of existing Section 301 duties and with product exemptions, and the 8-point gap to the 17% deal rate is effectively an incentive to close the agreement.

Markets wavered on Thursday: after Wednesday's 1,502-point (1.82%) jump to 83,938.28, the Sensex gave up 472 points from its opening level by 9:51 IST, and the Nifty fell to 25,734.60 (The Week, 26 Nov).

Foreign institutional investors bought ₹5,672.99 crore of shares on Monday 23 Nov and have put a record $14.28 billion into Indian equities this month, a shift attributed to investors leaving crowded global AI trades for a market with limited AI exposure.

stories.headline: RBI Staff Say Price Pressures Are Broadening as October Inflation Hits 6.1%, Ahead of a 4 December Policy Decision
stories.summary: An RBI staff paper on the state of the economy, released on 25 Nov, said inflation is becoming more generalised: headline CPI rose to 6.1% in October from 5.5% in September, and 11 of 12 divisions recorded sequential increases. The share of items with inflation above 4% and above 6% both rose, food and restaurant prices accelerated past 6%, and 11 states and union territories now have inflation above 6%. High-frequency data to 19 Nov point to continued broad food-price pressure. Most market watchers expect a 25-basis-point rate hike when the Monetary Policy Committee concludes its review on 4 Dec.
stories.market: A broadening of inflation strengthens the case for a December hike, pushing up short-dated Indian bond yields and weighing on rate-sensitive lenders and real-estate stocks.

body: The paper, published with the RBI's monthly bulletin, found that restaurants and accommodation and food and beverages had accelerated above 6%, while clothing, footwear and transport ran at 4-6%. Within food, vegetables, cereals, pulses and oils and fats all saw spikes.
Beyond the 11 states and union territories above 6%, another 20 had inflation between 4% and 6% in October, underlining how widespread the rise has become.

Staff said domestic growth drivers and macro fundamentals provide buffers, with activity indicators resilient in October on strong credit demand. Foreign-exchange reserves covered 10 months of goods imports as of 13 Nov and equalled 90.6% of external debt at end-June 2026.
The paper reflects the views of RBI staff, not the MPC, but it lands a week before the committee's December meeting.

stories.headline: Sugar Stocks Jump Up to 14% as Industry Body Forecasts a Decade-Low Crop of 26.5 Million Tonnes
stories.summary: The Indian Sugar & Bio-energy Manufacturers Association's preliminary estimate puts 2026-27 net sugar output at 26.5 million tonnes, a decade low and below 27.9 million last season, with gross output down about 15% from 31.21 million tonnes. Demand is estimated at 28-28.5 million tonnes, leaving consumption above production for the season, with no sugar diverted to ethanol. Poor monsoon rains and lower cane acreage in Maharashtra and Karnataka are the main causes; a closing stock of 3.6 million tonnes from 2025-26 provides an initial buffer. Dhampur Sugar rose 14% to ₹181.55, Uttam Sugar 12% and Shree Renuka 11% on the BSE by 10:14 IST on 26 Nov.

stories.headline: China Draws a 20% US Overcapacity Tariff Proposal, Halved for Some Goods and With Others Exempt, as Beijing Warns Against 'Political Manipulation'
stories.summary: USTR proposed on 25 Nov tariffs of up to 20% on Chinese goods outside its annexes and up to 10% on goods listed in Annex A, with Annex B goods exempt, tying the structure to the October 2025 Kuala Lumpur trade arrangement. The 20% applies net of the forced-labour Section 301 rate, and USTR said China could face up to 40% if its commitments prove unsatisfactory. Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said disputes should be settled through equal consultation, that overcapacity should not be a pretext for political manipulation, and urged both sides to implement their presidents' understandings. Hong Kong stocks rallied on Thursday morning, with the Hang Seng up more than 500 points through 22,500.
stories.market: The proposed 20%, level with Singapore and behind only Vietnam and India, sits within the truce framework, which helped Hong Kong tech and chip shares rebound on 26 Nov: SMIC rose over 4% and Alibaba and Meituan more than 4% in the morning session.

sources.name: Curtis, Mallet-Prevost trade law blog, 25 Nov

body: China's treatment is the most complex of the 14 economies: a top rate of up to 20% on goods not listed in the annexes, a lower rate of up to 10% on Annex A goods, and no new tariff on Annex B products. USTR said the rates reflect the arrangement reached in Kuala Lumpur on 30 Oct 2025.
If USTR judges Beijing's commitments unsatisfactory, the rate could rise to as much as 40%, the highest fallback among the targeted economies.

Beijing's initial response came from the foreign ministry rather than the commerce ministry, and was measured: Guo Jiakun called for consultation on the basis of equality and mutual benefit and for stable trade ties.

Hong Kong shares rose on Thursday morning after a sharp sell-off in chip and battery names on Wednesday: the Hang Seng opened 268 points higher and extended gains past 500 points, with Hua Hong and SMIC among the leaders (Longbridge, 26 Nov, early session).

On trade, USTR's 25 Nov notice proposed up to 15% on Japanese goods, net of MFN and existing Section 301 duties, rising to as much as 20% if Tokyo's commitments disappoint. stories.headline: Nvidia Slides Another 3.9% as Its Post-Reinstatement Rally Fades, With Huang Due Before House Panels on 1 December
stories.summary: Nvidia fell 3.91% on Wednesday 25 Nov, its second straight drop, giving back about 40% of Monday's 31.48% surge to $165.05 that followed Jensen Huang's reinstatement as chief executive; it had closed down 5.86% at $155.38 on Tuesday. The stock had closed at $125.53 on 20 Nov, 47.5% below its 6 Oct record close of $239.24. Huang, who resigned earlier this month over personal relationships including one with an executive alleged to have Chinese intelligence ties, faces closed-door House interviews on 1 Dec and a public Senate Banking hearing on export controls on 3 Dec. The Commerce Department's listing of chip partner Megaspeed and six affiliates on its Entity List was due in the Federal Register on 25 Nov.
stories.market: Nvidia's swings are driving the global chip complex; the Nasdaq 100 (QQQ) ended 0.65% lower on 25 Nov after being down 4.38% intraday, and US markets are shut today.

body: Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated Huang as CEO and president before the open on Monday 23 Nov, less than two weeks after he resigned. The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government that his return posed no national-security risk; President Trump said he had spoken with the board directly and indirectly. CFO Colette Kress had served as interim CEO for 12 days.

Monday's 31.48% gain added more than $900 billion in market value, after the company lost about $1.2 trillion while Huang was out. The rally then faded: the shares fell 5.86% on Tuesday and 3.91% on Wednesday, even as the broader market recovered most of a sharp morning sell-off.

Senate Banking Committee chair Tim Scott has scheduled the 3 Dec hearing under the title 'Protecting America's AI Advantage: Oversight of U.S. Export Controls'. Lawmakers want to know whether trade secrets were compromised and whether advanced chips were diverted to China through Singapore-based Megaspeed, which denies wrongdoing. Some members criticised the board for reinstating Huang before Congress heard from him.

Analysts remain split: Bernstein upgraded the stock to Outperform with a $200 target while flagging the investigations as a valuation cap, and William Blair pointed to unresolved governance, succession and regulatory questions.

stories.headline: US Blacklists Nvidia Partner Megaspeed and Six Affiliates, Including an Alibaba Unit, Over AI-Chip Diversion Risk
stories.summary: The Commerce Department has added seven companies in Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand to its Entity List over the risk that they are, or could become, involved in moving advanced AI chips to unauthorised buyers; the listing took effect on posting and was due in the Federal Register on 25 Nov. They include Singapore's Megaspeed International, which rents out computing power on Nvidia chips, and Apex Enterprise Solutions, Alibaba's Singapore subsidiary, which holds a security interest in Megaspeed's Malaysian affiliate Speedmatrix. US suppliers now need a licence, reviewed under a presumption of denial, to sell to the firms. Alibaba called its unit's listing erroneous and said it would pursue legal options.
stories.market: The listing tightens scrutiny of Southeast Asian AI-compute resellers; Alibaba's Hong Kong shares slipped 0.5% on 24 Nov but rose more than 4% on Thursday morning (26 Nov) in a broad tech rebound.

Megaspeed has been under US investigation since 2024 over possible diversion of chips to China. Speedmatrix reported about $2.14 billion in assets at the end of 2024.

stories.headline: Nvidia Agrees to Pay $290 Million to End the 2018 Shareholder Suit Over Crypto-Mining Sales
stories.summary: Nvidia agreed to pay $290 million in cash to settle a class action accusing it of hiding how much of its gaming revenue came from cryptocurrency miners, according to a filing in federal court in California (24 Nov). The class covers investors who bought the stock between 10 August 2017 and 15 November 2018; their damages expert put maximum recoverable damages at about $2.06 billion, so the deal is roughly 14% of that. Plaintiffs say Nvidia understated crypto-related GPU sales by about $1.1 billion over the period. The case reached the Supreme Court, which dismissed Nvidia's appeal in December 2024 without ruling. Nvidia denies wrongdoing.
stories.market: The sum is immaterial next to Nvidia's cash pile but removes a long-running overhang as chip stocks sold off this week. Plaintiffs' lawyers plan to seek up to 21.4%, about $62 million, in fees.

body: The settlement was filed for preliminary approval in the US District Court for the Northern District of California in In re Nvidia Corporation Securities Litigation (No. 4:18-cv-07669). A final approval hearing would follow roughly 130 days after preliminary approval and notice to investors.

Shareholders allege that in 2017-2018 miners bought large volumes of GeForce cards that Nvidia booked as gaming revenue, masking the company's dependence on a volatile crypto market. When mining demand collapsed, Nvidia cut its forecast in November 2018 and the stock fell about 28% over two sessions.

A district court dismissed the case in March 2021, but an appeals court revived claims against Nvidia and Jensen Huang in 2023. The Supreme Court heard argument and then dismissed Nvidia's appeal in December 2024, sending the case back for trial preparation. The class was certified in March 2026 and the parties accepted a mediator's proposal from former judge Layn Phillips in September.
Nvidia argues it could not reliably measure how much gaming revenue came from mining and is not admitting liability.

stories.headline: Musk Asks the Ninth Circuit to Throw Out the Twitter Fraud Verdict Valued at About $2.6 Billion
stories.summary: Elon Musk filed his opening brief with the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit (23 Nov, reported 24-25 Nov), asking it to overturn a March 2026 jury verdict that he defrauded Twitter shareholders with his May 2022 post saying the $44 billion takeover was 'temporarily on hold'. Twitter shares fell 9.7% to $40.72 that day. Class lawyers have valued the verdict at about $2.6 billion plus interest. Musk argues the investors never proved the price drop was caused by a false statement and challenges the class certification. The deadline for shareholders to file compensation claims passed on 24 Nov.
stories.market: A rare securities-fraud jury verdict against a chief executive; the appeal's outcome matters for how courts treat executives' social-media posts and for Musk's personal liquidity, much of it tied to Tesla (TSLA) shares.

body: The case, brought by a certified class of Twitter shareholders who sold while the deal was in doubt, was tried before US District Judge Charles Breyer in San Francisco. Jurors found in March 2026 that Musk's 13 May 2022 post was fraudulent; in July Breyer threw out findings on a second post but upheld the core verdict and denied a new trial and decertification.

In the Ninth Circuit brief, Musk argues the shareholders failed to tie the 9.7% share-price fall to any material falsity, that they are in effect seeking damages simply because the stock dropped, and that they did not show investors as a group relied on the post. He also attacks the class certification.

The shareholders say Musk used concerns about fake and spam accounts as a pretext to walk away or force a lower price. Musk ultimately closed the deal at the original $54.20 a share on 27 October 2022. Any payouts depend on the appeal; no argument date has been set.

stories.headline: Manhattan Judge Upholds New York's Rent Freeze on About a Million Stabilized Apartments
stories.summary: Justice Brendan Lantry of New York State Supreme Court dismissed a landlords' challenge (25 Nov) to the Rent Guidelines Board's June vote freezing rents on both one- and two-year renewals for rent-stabilized flats, the first freeze on two-year leases since the board began in 1969. The freeze, which took effect on 1 Oct and runs through 30 Sep 2027, covers roughly one million apartments. Lantry found the board had a rational basis and rejected claims that the 7-1 vote was rigged, while saying Mayor Zohran Mamdani had no power to freeze rents himself and calling his campaign pledge 'reckless'. The landlords can still appeal.
stories.market: The ruling keeps pressure on owners of rent-stabilized buildings, whose costs keep rising, and on banks with large New York multifamily loan books; the judge acknowledged the freeze may make refinancing and renovations harder.

body: Seven landlords, including members of Small Property Owners of New York and represented by former first deputy mayor Randy Mastro, argued that the mayor had packed the board with allies after promising a freeze, so the result was decided before any data on costs were weighed.

In a 20-page decision, Lantry said the board's 42-page explanatory statement addressed the factors the law requires, including the industry's economic condition and the cost of living, and that the freeze therefore stands. He rejected the collusion claims, noting that elections have consequences for who sits on the board.

He did criticise a pre-vote email in which the board chair shared a draft with a mayoral aide, saying it cast a shadow over the board's independence, but held it was not enough to overturn the order. Discovery produced about 1,000 documents; the petitioners never sought depositions.

The board had frozen one-year leases before, in 2015, 2016 and 2020. Separately, an appeals court revived the city's pied-a-terre tax on second homes worth $5 million or more about three weeks earlier.

stories.headline: Brussels and London Fine Givaudan, Firmenich and IFF About €570 Million for a Fragrance Cartel Aimed at Unilever
stories.summary: The European Commission fined three of the world's biggest fragrance makers a combined €471.9 million (25 Nov) for colluding on consumer and fine fragrances, with Givaudan hit for about €252.4 million, Firmenich €137.7 million and IFF about €82 million. Britain's Competition and Markets Authority added roughly £85 million in a coordinated decision, including just under £40 million for Givaudan, £20.6 million for Firmenich and about £24.6 million for IFF. Brussels says the conduct ran from March 2019 until dawn raids in March 2023 and centred on Unilever, the largest buyer of consumer fragrances: the firms swapped plans on price rises, negotiating tactics and energy surcharges and agreed not to poach each other's staff on the account. All three settled and received leniency and settlement reductions.
stories.market: Givaudan shares slipped about 2% in Zurich on the day (25 Nov); dsm-firmenich (DSFIR, Amsterdam) says it expects a total impact of about €300 million, mostly booked in 2026 and excluded from adjusted profit. The binding finding opens the door to follow-on damages claims from customers.

body: The European Commission and the UK Competition and Markets Authority closed their parallel fragrance cartel cases on 25 November with coordinated settlement decisions against Givaudan, Firmenich (now part of dsm-firmenich) and International Flavors & Fragrances. The EU total of €471.9 million (about $517 million) is the larger part; the CMA's fines add roughly £85 million, taking the combined bill to around €570 million.

According to the Commission, the companies coordinated for more than four years, from March 2019 until unannounced inspections in March 2023. The exchanges focused on Unilever and covered planned price increases, how to handle negotiations, possible energy surcharges and pushing back against the customer's requests for transparency on ingredient costs and formulas. The firms also agreed not to hire each other's staff working on the account. Senior people at Givaudan and IFF joined broader information exchanges from November 2021.

The fines reflect leniency reductions of between 20% and 50%, depending on when each firm came forward and how useful its evidence was, plus a further 10% for admitting liability under the settlement procedure. Firmenich received an extra 5% cut because its role in the wider exchanges was more limited.

dsm-firmenich said the authorities found Firmenich's involvement limited to exchanging information about one customer in its consumer fragrance business, that it did not involve price fixing, and that it predated the 2023 merger of DSM and Firmenich. It added that the US Justice Department closed its own probe of the company in February 2026 without findings, while inquiries in other jurisdictions continue.

Because a Commission cartel decision is binding proof of an infringement in national courts across the EU, buyers of fragrance ingredients may now pursue follow-on damages claims, a longer-term exposure not captured in the fines.

stories.headline: Shein Agrees to Pay $100 Million to Settle FTC Claims Over Late Deliveries, Hidden Reviews and Cotton Origins
stories.summary: The Federal Trade Commission filed a complaint and a proposed settlement in federal court in Los Angeles (24 Nov) under which Shein will pay $100 million for consumer refunds. The FTC alleges the retailer promised fast, reliable shipping while tens of thousands of shoppers got orders days, weeks or months late, suppressed critical reviews, and labelled cotton as US-grown when some came from China. It also says Shein, which ships nearly one million US packages a day, had only five phone customer-service agents as of September 2025. Shein said the deal is not an admission of liability.
stories.market: Shein listed in Hong Kong in September 2026; the settlement adds a compliance cost on top of the loss of US and EU de minimis duty exemptions and higher freight costs. Rival cross-border sellers such as PDD's Temu face the same rules on reviews and shipping notices.

body: The FTC voted 2-0 to file a complaint and a proposed stipulated order in the US District Court for the Central District of California. The order becomes binding once a judge signs it. The $100 million goes to the agency to fund redress for consumers.

The complaint cites Section 5 of the FTC Act, the Mail, Internet, or Telephone Order Merchandise Rule, which requires sellers to notify buyers of shipping delays, and the agency's newer rule on consumer reviews and testimonials. Beyond shipping, the FTC says Shein marketed its evoluSHEIN line as coming from suppliers that scored well on child- and forced-labour audits without producing any audit to back that up.

The proposed order bars Shein from misstating delivery times, suppressing negative reviews, failing to provide adequate customer service, and making deceptive claims about supplier audits or product traceability. Shein said it disagrees with parts of the FTC's description of its practices but has agreed to strengthen its compliance.

stories.summary: The Competition and Markets Authority said (25 Nov) that a remedy offered by AkzoNobel and Axalta could in principle resolve its concerns about UK vehicle refinish coatings, the paint used in body shops. The companies offered on 18 Nov to sell AkzoNobel's European vehicle refinish business, matching the package agreed with the European Commission, after the CMA flagged problems on 11 Nov. The merger would create a coatings group with about $17 billion of revenue and the companies expect completion by early 2027.

stories.headline: EU Ambassadors Take Up a 22nd Russia Package That Would Cut 60 Banks From SWIFT and Ban Russian-Insured Tankers
stories.summary: EU ambassadors held their first discussion (25 Nov) of the Commission's 22nd sanctions package, unveiled by Ursula von der Leyen late on 23 Nov. It would put about 60 Russian banks under a transaction ban and remove them all from SWIFT, list more than 70 further shadow-fleet vessels, and bar every tanker insured in Russia. European firms would also be barred from building, operating or repairing Russian energy infrastructure, notably refineries, with electricity services covered for the first time. The package needs the backing of all 27 member states.
stories.market: A ban on Russian-insured tankers would hit the shadow fleet's main workaround for Western insurance, a factor for Urals discounts and tanker rates; the refinery-services ban lands as Ukrainian strikes have already cut Russian processing. European banks and oil-service firms with residual Russian links face new compliance work.

body: The proposal builds on a fast run of financial measures: 20 banks were put under a transaction ban in the 20th package in April, 33 were cut from SWIFT in the 21st in July, and ambassadors agreed listings for 50 more banks earlier in November. The new step would take the transaction ban to about 60 banks, all disconnected from SWIFT.

On energy, EU companies could no longer help build, run or repair Russian energy infrastructure, including refineries, and the ban on services would for the first time cover electricity. Foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said dozens more energy-sector actors, including shadow-fleet enablers, would be listed and export bans tightened for LNG and oil projects. Ministers had already blacklisted the Ust-Luga gas complex and several large refineries on 16 November.

The package also targets crypto and payment channels in Russia and in third countries used to dodge sanctions; the Commission is reported to be preparing a blanket ban on crypto platforms in Kyrgyzstan. Georgia's Kulevi refinery would be delisted because it now runs Libyan rather than Russian crude.

Non-financial measures include an entry ban on Russian ex-combatants who fought in Ukraine, a bar on Europeans sitting on the boards of companies in Russia, and restrictions on Russian teams, symbols and sponsorship money at EU sports and cultural events. Adoption requires unanimity among the 27 governments.

stories.headline: US Adds 31 Names to Its Sanctions List, From Cuban Banks to 'Ndrangheta-Linked Firms, as a Russian Procurement Agent Pleads Guilty
stories.summary: The State Department and Treasury's OFAC published four Federal Register notices (24 Nov) formally adding 31 designees, 15 people and 16 entities, to the Specially Designated Nationals list. The State listings target Cuban mining, energy and banking bodies, including Banco Exterior de Cuba and Banco Internacional de Comercio; OFAC's notice covers networks tied to the Italian 'Ndrangheta and the Comanchero motorcycle gang, including Canadian funeral-home and limousine companies. Separately, Russian national Alexander Suvorov pleaded guilty (24 Nov) to conspiring to export US dual-use electronics to Russia through Hong Kong front companies between March 2022 and April 2023.
stories.market: Banks and payment firms must now screen and block transactions involving the two Cuban banks; the actions add to a week of US pressure on illicit finance alongside the Iran shadow-banking designations of 23 Nov.

sources.name: CASRAI summary of Federal Register notices, 24 Nov

body: Three of the notices come from the State Department under Executive Order 14404 and cover Cuba. They list a family member of Alejandro Castro Espin, state companies in nickel mining and petroleum (including Comercial CUPET), a nickel research centre in Moa, and two banks, Banco Exterior de Cuba and Banco Internacional de Comercio (BICSA). The underlying actions date from September and October; publication makes them part of the official record.

The OFAC notice, under Executive Order 14059 on narcotics trafficking and signed on 19 November, names 14 individuals and six entities linked to the 'Ndrangheta and the Comanchero outlaw motorcycle gang, among them four Canadian funeral and limousine businesses.

In the criminal case, Suvorov, 52, a Russian national who lived in Sweden, admitted conspiring to violate the Export Control Reform Act. Prosecutors in the Northern District of New York say he maintained Hong Kong front companies, including GS Group Limited, to hide the Russian end users of components that can be used in military communications and radar; wire payments to US suppliers exceeded $70,000. He faces up to 20 years in prison at sentencing on 29 March 2027.

stories.headline: Rial Crashes Through 2.9 Million per Dollar, a Record Low, Two Days After New US Shadow-Banking Sanctions
stories.summary: The US dollar fetched more than 2.9 million rials in Tehran's open market on Wednesday 25 Nov, a fresh record low for the Iranian currency, after first touching about 2.83 million earlier in the day. A day earlier (24 Nov) the street dollar had been quoted near 2.82 million, up about 5% from roughly 2.68 million. The slide followed US Treasury sanctions on 23 Nov against an Iranian network of exchange houses and the continued US blockade that has squeezed Iran's oil revenue. Reports noted several weeks of relative calm before the sudden drop.

stories.headline: Baghdad Seizes Control of Kurdish Border Crossings as a Leaked Report Traces Smuggled Crude to Iran and Afghanistan
stories.summary: Iraq's Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi ordered on 24 Nov that the Kurdistan Regional Government export oil only via the federal Oil Ministry, that federal authorities take over all Kurdistan border crossings, and that the ministry run oilfields in disputed parts of Kirkuk, Nineveh, Diyala and Salahuddin. The order followed a leaked federal intelligence report, based on 2023-26 satellite imagery, describing Kirkuk crude trucked via Kurdistan to Iran, blended and relabelled, and sold onward in Afghanistan. Iraq's Supreme Court on 25 Nov backed federal control of borders, customs and oil oversight, while Kurdish leaders called the move unconstitutional. The National Security Service reported two further anti-smuggling operations on 25 Nov, including a tapped pipeline south of Baghdad, extending a campaign that began with oil theft documented at Jurf Al Sakhar from 2021-26.
stories.market: Tighter federal control could, over time, curb leakage of Iraqi crude into grey channels serving sanctioned Iran, but the Baghdad-Erbil clash adds risk to northern exports and Kurdistan-focused oil producers.

body: The leaked document, the second in a week, was compiled by the geospatial intelligence unit of Iraq's Federal Intelligence and Investigations Agency and describes two main routes for diverted crude: an eastern one through Kurdistan into Iran and on to Afghanistan, and a northern one toward the Turkish border with reissued shipping papers.

An earlier leak concerned Jurf Al Sakhar, south of Baghdad, where investigators say hundreds of millions of dollars of state oil was siphoned off; nine senior security and oil officials were dismissed and security forces moved in after Kataib Hezbollah, which denies the allegations, was ordered out.
Kurdish leaders rejected Baghdad's orders, with Masoud Barzani calling them reckless, and local reports said Peshmerga units were being sent toward the boundary with federal territory.

key_figures.label: Disputed provinces placed under Oil Ministry

stories.headline: Chainflip Puts Its Vault Loss at About $12 Million as Most Funds Move Through Tornado Cash; Bitcoin Miners Hit by Hashrate Hijacking
stories.summary: Cross-chain exchange Chainflip expanded its estimate of the 21 Nov theft from its vaults to roughly $12 million in BTC, ETH, USDC and USDT, from an initial $4.86 million, and offered the attacker a 10% bounty for returning 90%, with a deadline of 23 Nov; most of the stolen funds had been moved into the Tornado Cash mixer. Separately, mining-pool operator Braiins said on 25 Nov that an ongoing campaign had diverted up to 1.9 EH/s of bitcoin hashrate, targeting more than 1,000 mining sites on 20 Nov, spreading from Latin America to Europe.
stories.market: Chainflip's FLIP token fell about 43% after disclosure; the mining attacks add operational risk for listed miners still exposed to unencrypted pool connections.

stories.headline: New York Wins a $1.37 Billion Judgment Against NovaTech's Founders as China Announces a $2.25 Billion Deposit-Fraud Suspect Extradited by Russia
stories.summary: New York Attorney General Letitia James said on 25 Nov she had won a $1,367,023,585 judgment against Cynthia and Eddy Petion, founders of crypto trading firm NovaTechFx, over a Ponzi and pyramid scheme that drew hundreds of thousands of investors worldwide, including about 11,000 New Yorkers, many from Haitian and immigrant communities. The couple, who fled the country, were already banned from the securities, commodities and crypto industries by an August 2025 default judgment; four promoters separately paid nearly $6 million. Also on 25 Nov, China's Ministry of Public Security announced that Russia had extradited a suspect surnamed Shu, accused of illegally taking more than 15 billion yuan (about $2.25 billion) in public deposits through fabricated wealth products.
stories.market: Large judgments against absent defendants rarely translate into full recoveries; both cases add to the regulatory focus on unlicensed high-yield products and crypto-based schemes.

stories.headline: Wall Street Braces for December Redemption Data From the Five Biggest Private-Credit Funds as a Pension Weighs a $4 Billion Fund-Stake Financing
stories.summary: Quarterly redemption figures from non-traded private-credit funds, due in early December, could set the tone for alternative asset managers, Wells Fargo Securities said, flagging the funds of Blackstone, Blue Owl, Apollo, HPS and Ares as the five largest; their fourth-quarter tender offers expire in the coming weeks. Separately, a major US pension is weighing raising about $4 billion through a rare financing that bundles its stakes in private-credit funds run by Blackstone, Blue Owl and others, according to a Bloomberg report summarised by MT Newswires on 25 Nov. Redemption requests have run above normal through 2026; across 19 NAV BDCs, third-quarter requests equalled 11.5% of tender-offer NAV, down from 12.7% in the second quarter, per Robert A. Stanger & Co.

stories.headline: RBI Flags Non-Bank Lenders' Growing Reliance on Bank Loans, Now 39.6% of Their Borrowings
stories.summary: Bank loans made up 39.6% of Indian non-bank lenders' borrowings at end-March 2026, up from 35.3% four years earlier, according to an RBI study in its November bulletin published on 25 Nov. Bank borrowings rose 24.6% in 2025-26 to ₹19.43 trillion, outpacing total NBFC borrowings, which grew 17.9% to ₹49.04 trillion, while the share of debentures fell to 34.1% from 40%. The RBI said the trend needs ongoing monitoring for systemic risk. It partly attributed the shift to lower risk weights on bank lending to NBFCs, and said overseas borrowings had risen to 11% of NBFC funding from 6.9% in March 2022.
stories.market: Deeper bank-NBFC links raise contagion risk between India's banks and shadow lenders; watch NBFC stocks and bank exposure disclosures, with the Nifty Financial Services index in focus.

stories.headline: Carlyle Affiliate Named as the Seller of 7.4% of Piramal Pharma; LG Puts Up to 2% of Its Indian Arm on the Block
stories.summary: Exchange data show Carlyle affiliate CA Alchemy Investments sold more than 9.86 crore Piramal Pharma shares, a 7.41% stake, on 25 Nov at an average Rs 224.17, raising about Rs 2,211.55 crore and cutting its holding to 10.52% from 17.93%. Mutual funds run by Aditya Birla Sun Life and Axis were among the buyers at about Rs 224.10. On 26 Nov South Korea's LG Electronics began selling up to 1.36 crore shares, or 2%, of LG Electronics India at a floor of Rs 1,709.30, about 6% below the prior close, a deal worth up to Rs 2,320.5 crore. LG Electronics India fell nearly 3% in early trade (26 Nov).
stories.market: Both blocks were absorbed by domestic institutions, a sign local funds still have cash to deploy; the LG sale reduces the parent's stake to 83% from 85% and moves it toward India's minimum public-float rule.

body: The Piramal Pharma block that knocked the stock down as much as 7% on 25 Nov came from CA Alchemy Investments, an affiliate of Carlyle Group. It sold 7.41% of the drugmaker at an average of Rs 224.17 a share for about Rs 2,211.55 crore, leaving it with 10.52%. Funds managed by Aditya Birla Sun Life and Axis bought shares at about Rs 224.10.

On 26 Nov LG Electronics Inc launched a block sale of up to 13.58 million shares of its listed Indian unit on the NSE at a floor of Rs 1,709.30, roughly a 6% discount. The proceeds go to the parent, which agreed to a 180-day lock-up on further sales. A full sale would take its stake from 85% to 83%, helping it meet SEBI's minimum public shareholding rules.
Separately, Quality Power Electrical Equipments opened a qualified institutional placement on 25 Nov with a floor price of Rs 1,535.53 and the option of a discount of up to 5%.

stories.headline: Crystal Crop Protection Lists at a Modest 2-3% Premium Despite 17-Times Demand; Tokyo's TOKIUM Opens 8% Below Its Price
stories.summary: Crystal Crop Protection's shares opened at Rs 278 on the NSE and Rs 280 on the BSE on 26 Nov, 2.2-2.9% above the Rs 272 IPO price, after its Rs 455.49 crore offer was subscribed 17.07 times. Non-institutional investors bid 37.70 times their allotment and institutions 15.47 times. Foodlink F&B Holdings opened its IPO for subscription the same day, and PhonePe has restarted its IPO process, targeting a February-March listing at a valuation of up to Rs 1.5 lakh crore. In Tokyo, expense-software firm TOKIUM priced at the top of its range at ¥1,620 but opened 8.0% below it (25 Nov).
stories.market: Muted debuts despite heavy subscription show IPO investors are trimming listing-day expectations as Asian tech sells off; no major US IPOs priced in the holiday week.

body: Crystal Crop Protection, an agrochemicals maker, raised Rs 455.49 crore through a Rs 355 crore fresh issue and an offer for sale of up to Rs 101 crore by promoter Ankur Aggarwal. Bids covered 20.77 crore shares against 1.22 crore on offer, a 17.07-times subscription, with retail investors at 9.28 times.
Despite that demand the stock opened only slightly above the Rs 272 issue price on 26 Nov, at Rs 278 on the NSE and Rs 280 on the BSE.
The pipeline remains busy: Foodlink F&B Holdings opened its offer on 26 Nov, and digital-payments company PhonePe has revived its listing plans with a February-March target.

In Japan, TOKIUM priced at ¥1,620, the top of its range, on strong book demand, yet opened 8% lower on 25 Nov as tech stocks across Asia fell. In the US no major IPOs or large follow-ons were reported ahead of Thanksgiving.
